input:
A gravity settler is a widely used item of equipment whose purpose is to remove solid particles from a liquid stream by allowing them to settle out under the influence of gravity, and in the present case the settler is required to remove sand from a process stream. The sizing of such a unit is commonly approached through the design overflow rate, which is the throughput of liquid divided by the plan area of the settler, and which effectively represents the upward velocity of the liquid that the settling particles have to overcome. For this particular duty, the design overflow rate has been set at 0.69 m h-1, and the settler is required to handle a throughput of 141 m3 h-1. Dividing the throughput by the design overflow rate in order to obtain the required area, the plan area of the settler works out at 204 m2.

It is very important to appreciate the basis on which this sizing rests. The design overflow rate adopted here does not come from any experimental work carried out on the material in question; instead, it is a vendor rule that is customarily applied to this solid. Moreover, no settling test has actually been run on the real slurry that the settler will have to treat, which means that the settling behaviour of the sand in the actual process liquid has never been directly observed or measured. The resulting area should therefore be regarded as an estimate that is founded upon a general rule of thumb for this kind of solid, rather than as a figure that has been verified against the behaviour of the specific slurry concerned, and some caution is accordingly appropriate when the result is carried forward into subsequent design work.
target:
A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. The liquid passes slowly enough through the vessel for the sand to fall to the bottom while the clarified liquid leaves over the top. Settler sizing turns on the overflow rate, the throughput divided by the plan area of the vessel: the overflow rate is the upward velocity of the liquid in the settler, and particles settle out against it where their own settling velocity exceeds it.

The design overflow rate for this duty is 0.69 m h-1 and the throughput is 141 m3 h-1. Division of the throughput by the overflow rate gives the plan area: 204 m2.

Two features of the sizing deserve stating. The plan area, not the vessel volume, is the dimension the calculation returns: depth is set by other considerations, by the room the settled sand needs and by the flow distribution the inlet can achieve, and a deeper vessel of the same area settles no more sand. The overflow rate is also the settler's operating limit, not only its design figure: throughput pushed above the design value raises the upward velocity in the same proportion, and the particles that settled at the design rate are the first to be carried over the top when the rate rises.

The limit on the result stands in its basis. The design overflow rate is a vendor rule for this solid, not a measured property of the slurry the settler will treat, and no settling test has been run on the actual slurry. A settling test would return the rate from the slurry's own behaviour in the process liquid; the vendor rule stands in for that measurement, on the strength of the vendor's experience with the solid in other liquids. The plan area is therefore a rule-based estimate. It is fit for layout and cost work at this stage, and the settler should not be committed to fabrication until a settling test on the actual slurry has either confirmed the rate or replaced it.
